archetype.name: Pocket Passer (timing and precision)
archetype.definition: Burrow wins from the pocket with anticipation and ball placement rather than arm-talent shots or his legs: he throws on time, completes far more than expected and does his damage on throws between 10 and 20 yards.

report.headline: Burrow's accuracy is back at its 2024 level, carried by intermediate throws.
report.take:
Burrow is what he has been in his best seasons: a rhythm passer whose edge is completion percentage over expected. His 7.05 CPOE ranks 3rd of 45, in line with his 2021 and 2024 seasons (both near the top of the league in that stat). This is not a new player. It is the healthy version of a known one, running the most pass-heavy offense in football in neutral situations (pass rate over expected rank 1 of 32). The volume comes with the scheme, and his perGame touchdown rate leads the position.

The production comes almost entirely from one band of the field. Throws of 10+ air yards have added 74.1 EPA. Everything under 10 yards is net negative at -12, and throws behind the line alone cost -15.1. The intermediate game (0.944 EPA per attempt, 17.7 CPOE on 48 throws) is the engine, and Tee Higgins (0.74 EPA per target on 50 targets) and Mike Gesicki are cashing it. Meanwhile the screen-and-checkdown game to Chase Brown has been a real drain at -0.383 per target. The offense is efficient despite its short game, not because of it.

What the season line hides is how it started. Weeks 1 and 2 were negative-EPA games, the Houston game included five sacks and a 19.4% bad-throw rate. Since then each game has been strongly positive, and the last three sit at 0.332 EPA per dropback with an 11.2 CPOE and a 2.5% sack rate. He has adjusted to a line that allows hits (team hit rate rank 26) by getting the ball out. Aggressiveness is down 4.2 points from last year and time to throw is quicker. His pressure-to-sack rate of 20% is the best of his career. The bad-throw jump versus last year looks scary, but last season's 5% was the outlier; his 11% matches 2024.

Going forward, the ceiling is the 2024 season, and the pace is tracking it almost exactly. Expect the 1.601 EPA per deep attempt on 18 throws to cool, and the intermediate CPOE to come down some. The underlying skill and the pass-first role are durable, though, so a drop from 'excellent' to 'very good' is the realistic regression, not a collapse.

strengths.title: Intermediate accuracy drives the offense
strengths.body: His throws of 10-19 air yards are landing at a 75% clip with a 17.7 CPOE, and that band alone accounts for most of his passing value. This is his career calling card: timing throws to Higgins and Gesicki over linebackers and under safeties. The rate will drift down, but the skill has held across seasons.

strengths.title: Beating pressure by getting rid of it
strengths.body: Behind a line that gives up hits, he has cut his pressure-to-sack rate to 20%, well below his usual 30%-plus. He is holding the ball less and taking fewer low-percentage shots. The last three games pushed his sack rate down to 2.5%. It's a deliberate trade of some aggressiveness for clean, on-schedule football, and it fits who he is.

strengths.title: Two receivers producing at once
strengths.body: Higgins and Ja'Marr Chase have both produced strongly per target on heavy volume, so defenses can't roll coverage to one side. Gesicki's 1.018 EPA per target on 18 looks is a small sample but a useful third option over the middle. That target structure is stable as long as the receivers stay healthy.

concerns.title: The short game is dead weight
concerns.body: Throws behind the line have lost 15.1 EPA, and the checkdowns to Chase Brown are costing points every time. All three of his interceptions came on throws under 10 yards. This is partly scheme and partly the back. Either way it makes the offense lean on explosive intermediate and deep throws, and those are the most volatile plays in football.

concerns.title: Deep efficiency on a tiny sample
concerns.body: His 1.601 EPA per deep attempt with a 24 CPOE comes on just 18 throws, and four of them went for touchdowns. That will not hold. Because his aggressiveness is down, he doesn't have the deep volume to absorb a cold stretch either.

concerns.title: Protection can still break down
concerns.body: The offense ranks 26th in hit rate allowed. Houston showed the downside: five sacks and his worst accuracy game of the year. His quick release masks the problem against most fronts, but a good pass rush can still take games away from him.

trend.note: His first two games added negative EPA, and every game since has been clearly positive. The bye-week return at Baltimore (18.2 EPA, 15.5 CPOE) was his best of the year. The last three games run 0.109 EPA per dropback above his season mark.

nextGame.headline: Soft Titans pass defense, but a blowout could cap volume
nextGame.body:
Tennessee's pass defense ranks 24th in EPA allowed, 26th on explosive passes and 26th on short throws, and it has let opposing WR1s score well above their usual output. That lines up with Burrow's intermediate game and with Higgins' lead role. The catch is twofold. Offenses run more than usual against the Titans (passRateOverNorm rank 31), and only three defenses allow fewer QB touchdowns per game. The tight end spot, where Gesicki has been efficient, is also one of the areas Tennessee covers well.

The bigger script factor is the Titans' offense, which ranks 31st in EPA and will be without Calvin Ridley and Tyjae Spears. A 10-point spread and a -600 moneyline point to Cincinnati leading comfortably. In games where Burrow has led by 9+, his efficiency has dipped below zero, and he played only 94% of snaps in the Baltimore blowout. On his own side, Erick All Jr. (knee, questionable) and Tanner Hudson (IR) leave the tight end room thin behind Gesicki. That matters more for blocking than for targets.

keyMatchups.title: Higgins against a generous WR1 matchup
keyMatchups.body: Tennessee ranks 28th in how far it lets WR1s outscore their averages and 22nd in EPA per target to that role. Higgins leads the team in targets and has been the most efficient receiver on volume. Expect intermediate throws to him to be the main path.

keyMatchups.title: Blowout script versus pass volume
keyMatchups.body: The Titans' offense is among the league's worst and is missing two skill players, so Cincinnati could be playing with a big lead early. His efficiency fades in those states, and attempts likely drop in the second half.

keyMatchups.title: Touchdowns may come on the ground
keyMatchups.body: Tennessee gives up yards to quarterbacks but few touchdowns, and offenses tend to run on it. Red-zone trips could end in Chase Brown carries rather than Burrow throws, which tempers his touchdown upside even in a favorable matchup.

nextGame.watch: Whether Cincinnati keeps throwing after it builds a lead, or turns the second half over to the run game.

restOfSeason.body:
The parts that should last are the role, the accuracy and the release. Cincinnati passes more than anyone in neutral situations, his CPOE matches his best seasons, and getting the ball out quickly protects him behind a shaky line. Expect a passer who rarely has a bad game and posts around 260-300 yards with two-plus touchdowns most weeks. The early-season Houston game is the template for his down weeks: a fast rush, not mistakes he creates.

The parts that will cool are the deep efficiency on 18 attempts and some of the intermediate hit rate. If the screen game to Brown stays this bad, there is no cushion when the explosive throws dry up. I'd project efficiency settling around 0.15-0.25 EPA per dropback, still a top-10 level. Touchdowns should drift toward the lower end of a high range rather than holding at the current league-leading rate.
swingFactors: Pass protection holding up against good pass rushes
Whether the short and screen game stops costing points

confidence.note: Six games, a small deep-ball sample, but the accuracy profile matches his best seasons.
